marking_points.credit_text: limited liability identified and correctly stated
conjunctive_conditions: states that the owner’s liability is limited
states that it is the owner’s personal assets that are protected
accept: the owner can only lose what was invested in the company
marking_points.notes: The conjunctive pair separates a memorised phrase from understanding.

marking_points.credit_text: a second accurate advantage identified
alternatives: shares may be sold to family and friends to raise capital
the company has a separate legal identity, so it continues if the owner dies
suppliers and lenders often treat an incorporated business as lower risk

marking_points.credit_text: the advantage is tied to the circumstances of a small family bakery
accept: ovens or premises are the bakery’s main asset and would otherwise be at risk
family members are the likely source of new share capital
reject: repeats the word bakery without a fact that is true only of a bakery
marking_points.notes: Cover-the-name test applies to the stem context.

marking_points.credit_text: a causal link from limited liability to a consequence for the owner
conjunctive_conditions: names the risk the owner faces as a sole trader
states the consequence of that risk being removed
accept: unlimited liability means the family home could be sold to pay a debt, so incorporation removes that exposure and makes the owner willing to borrow for a second oven

marking_points.credit_text: a causal link from the second advantage to a consequence for the business
accept: share capital costs no interest, so cash that would have serviced a loan pays for stock instead

marker_notes: Two advantages are required. A third advantage earns nothing; a second link on either advantage earns AN2.
common_errors: Confusing limited liability with limited debt.
Claiming a private limited company can sell shares on a stock exchange.

marking_points.credit_text: motivators correctly identified
alternatives: achievement
recognition
responsibility
the work itself
advancement
marking_points.notes: One motivator named accurately is enough for K1.

marking_points.credit_text: hygiene factors correctly distinguished from motivators
conjunctive_conditions: names at least one hygiene factor
states that hygiene factors remove dissatisfaction rather than create satisfaction

marking_points.credit_text: the theory is applied to call-centre work
accept: agents follow a script and escalate anything unusual, so the work itself offers little achievement
call handling is measured by average handling time, so recognition is currently for speed only
reject: says only that call centre staff need motivating

marking_points.credit_text: a causal link from a named motivator to a workplace outcome
accept: widening the value an agent may refund without escalation gives responsibility, so agents resolve calls themselves, which shortens queues

marking_points.credit_text: a second link, or a link explaining why improving a hygiene factor alone will not raise motivation
accept: a pay rise stops complaints about pay but leaves the work unchanged, so turnover returns to its old level within months

marker_notes: Credit the theory used, not the theory named. Listing Herzberg’s factors with no call-centre consequence caps the answer at K1 and K2.
common_errors: Treating pay as a motivator.
Describing Maslow instead.

marking_points.credit_text: niche marketing accurately defined
conjunctive_conditions: identifies a small, specific segment of the market
identifies that the product is tailored to that segment
accept: aims at a narrow group with particular needs rather than at the whole market

marking_points.credit_text: a relevant reason identified
alternatives: less direct competition in the segment
customers in the niche are less price sensitive
promotion can be targeted, so less is wasted
the mass market is saturated or shrinking

marking_points.credit_text: first chain: reason to mechanism to effect
accept: fewer direct rivals in the high-protein segment means demand is less price sensitive, so the firm can hold a premium price and raise contribution per box

marking_points.credit_text: second chain on a different reason
accept: targeting one segment cuts wasted advertising, so the promotional budget per sale falls and the lower volume still covers fixed costs

marking_points.credit_text: either chain extended to a further consequence for the business
accept: higher contribution per box lowers break-even output, so the firm survives a fall in supermarket orders

marker_notes: Analyse is capped at AO3. A concluding judgement earns nothing here (05-PROC-004).
common_errors: Describing niche marketing without saying what follows from it.
Writing an evaluation the command word does not ask for.

marking_points.credit_text: quality control accurately described as inspection of output after production
accept: faults are found by inspectors at the end of the line

marking_points.credit_text: TQM accurately described
conjunctive_conditions: quality is built in during the process rather than inspected at the end
every employee is responsible for the quality of their own work

marking_points.credit_text: the difference is applied to components manufacture
accept: a defective brake component found by the customer triggers a recall, so detection at the press rather than at final inspection matters
reject: repeats the phrase car components factory with no fact particular to it

marking_points.credit_text: a causal link from earlier detection to a cost or waste consequence
accept: a fault caught at the press is scrapped as one part, so reworking a finished assembly is avoided and material waste falls

marking_points.credit_text: a second link, including a link to the cost of introducing TQM
accept: TQM needs every operator trained, so unit costs rise before they fall and the payback takes a year or more

common_errors: Treating TQM as a stricter form of inspection.
Claiming TQM removes all quality costs.

marking_points.credit_text: fixed and variable costs both defined against output
conjunctive_conditions: fixed cost does not vary with output over the relevant range
variable cost changes directly with output

marking_points.credit_text: contribution per unit defined as selling price minus variable cost per unit
chain from contribution to a pricing floor
accept: any price above variable cost adds contribution, so in a slack month an order priced below full cost still helps pay the rent

marking_points.credit_text: chain from spreading fixed costs to average cost and price
accept: fixed cost per table falls as the workshop fills, so a lower price can still be profitable at higher volume

marking_points.credit_text: either chain extended to break-even or margin of safety
accept: a lower contribution per table raises break-even output, so the workshop must sell more before it makes any profit

common_errors: Pricing below variable cost and calling it contribution.
Treating average cost as if it were constant.

indicative_content.text: Profit maximisation defined as choosing the output and price at which total revenue exceeds total cost by the largest amount, not simply making a profit.
Alternative objectives available to a new business: survival, cash generation, market share, sales growth, social or environmental objectives.
Cash, not profit, is what kills new businesses: a start-up meeting payroll from a shrinking bank balance needs a survival objective even while it is profitable on paper.
Pricing to maximise short-run profit can lose the market share that a young business needs before rivals enter; penetration pricing sacrifices margin to build a customer base.
Investors and lenders in the first three years usually look at growth and cash burn, so an objective set for a bank may differ from one set for the founders.
The judgement turns on the funding position and the market: a business with committed funding and a defensible niche can pursue profit early, one dependent on an overdraft cannot.
Objectives are not permanent. A defensible answer states when the business should change objective and what signal should trigger the change.

marker_notes: AO2 requires a named business with facts specific to it. "A small business" is not application.
common_errors: Listing objectives without deciding between them.
Confusing profit maximisation with revenue maximisation.

indicative_content.text: Democratic, autocratic, paternalistic and laissez-faire styles defined by where the decision is made and how far employees are consulted.
Consultation raises the quality of a decision where employees hold information the manager does not, and raises acceptance of the decision once made.
Consultation is slow. Where change is forced by a deadline — a regulator, a failing supplier, a cash shortfall — the cost of delay can exceed the benefit of consent.
Tannenbaum and Schmidt: style is a continuum, and the appropriate point depends on the time available, the competence of the team and the consequences of being wrong.
Change resisted is change that fails; force-field analysis frames the driving and restraining forces a leader must move.
A defensible judgement separates the decision from its implementation: an autocratic decision announced with a democratic implementation is common and often effective.
The decisive factor is usually urgency and the skill level of the workforce; a strong answer names which one is doing the work in its chosen example.

common_errors: Answering "always" as if the word were not in the question.
Describing styles without applying any to change.

Cost leadership requires scale and process investment; Halvara makes industrial units in low volumes, so the scale economies that would deliver it are not available at $46m of revenue.
A 6% operating margin leaves almost no room to cut price: a 3% price cut removes half the operating profit before any volume arrives.
Differentiation in refrigeration is defensible on energy efficiency, service response and compliance with tightening standards, and it earns a price the current margin badly needs.
Gearing of 58% and retained profit of $1.9m against a $12m expansion mean the strategy chosen must be one lenders will fund; a price war funded by debt is the least fundable option.

indicative_content.text: Sources of long-term finance: retained profit, rights issue or new equity, bank loan, corporate bond, leasing, sale and leaseback, venture or private equity.
Retained profit of $1.9m funds about one sixth of $12m, so internal finance alone cannot do it and the question is which external source, not whether.
Gearing already at 58% means further debt raises interest cover risk on a 6% margin; a rise in rates would take the margin before it takes the expansion.
New equity avoids the interest commitment but dilutes family control, which for a family-controlled group is a strategic cost, not only a financial one.
Leasing or sale and leaseback of plant matches the payment to the life of the asset and keeps the debt off the balance sheet in part, at a higher total cost.
Phasing the expansion — funding stage one from retained profit plus a modest loan and stage two from the cash the first stage generates — reduces the peak requirement and the peak gearing.
A recommendation must name the mix, the amount from each source and the timing; Recommend is not satisfied by a preference.
The justification should turn on the family’s willingness to dilute against the group’s ability to service debt at a 6% margin, and should state the condition under which the recommendation changes.

indicative_content.text: Leadership styles and the continuum between them; the distinction between leadership and management; Handy or Mintzberg on organisational culture and structure.
The two firms have opposite decision-making cultures, so the merger is a culture clash before it is a structural one, and the leader chooses which culture survives.
Announcing 40 redundancies raises resistance; a consultative style raises acceptance but takes weeks the January move does not allow.
Force-field analysis: the driving force is cost saving, the restraining forces are fear of job loss and loss of autonomy in the pods, and leadership acts mainly on the restraining side.
Other factors compete for importance: the integration plan and its timetable, retention of key client relationships, the IT and process merge, and whether the cost savings were realistic.
In a people business of 900 staff the asset that can leave is the staff; if the best pod leaders resign in the first quarter the savings are lost whatever the plan says.
Assess requires a weighing: leadership style is necessary but not sufficient, and the answer should say what it is being weighed against and which factor dominates in this case.
A conclusion that names a condition — leadership matters most in the first six months, the integration plan thereafter — earns the contextual judgement.

indicative_content.text: Standardisation and adaptation as the two poles of international marketing strategy; pan-national segments; the four elements of the mix that can be adapted independently.
Standardisation holds the $11 contribution per unit by keeping one formulation, one filling run and one set of packaging artwork.
Adaptation adds cost at every stage: separate registration of a cosmetic formulation, separate label translation and separate minimum production runs, all recovered over smaller volumes.
Regulation is not optional: where a market restricts an ingredient or requires local labelling, the choice to adapt has already been made for the business.
A plant-based positioning may itself be the pan-national segment, so the customer Solara is chasing may be more alike across borders than the countries are.
Distribution is through pharmacies, whose buyers differ by country in what they list and at what price, so place and price may need adapting even where the product does not.
A defensible answer separates the elements: standardise the product, adapt the promotion and the price, and say why that split fits a firm that has never traded outside its region.
The judgement should name the deciding condition — regulatory difference and pharmacy buying practice — rather than resting on cost alone.

Discussing exporting in general rather than this decision.

indicative_content.text: Corporate planning as the cycle of objectives, strategic analysis, choice, implementation and review; contingency planning and scenario planning as variants.
Fuel at 31% of operating costs means a plan built on one fuel price is a plan built on the largest uncertainty Talaria faces; scenario planning addresses that directly.

Emissions rules tightening within three years are known, dated and unavoidable, so this part of the environment is exactly what a corporate plan is good at: a fleet replacement decision needs a three-year horizon.
Gearing of 60% means fleet renewal must be scheduled against debt capacity rather than bought when rules bite, which is a planning problem, not a reactive one.
The cost of planning is real: management time, and the risk that a plan written around one fuel scenario becomes a commitment nobody will abandon.
Long-distance contracts are themselves multi-year commitments, so Talaria has already accepted a planning horizon whether or not it writes a plan.

The judgement should separate the parts of the environment: planning is most useful for the known and dated (emissions rules, fleet age) and least useful for the volatile (fuel prices), where contingency planning replaces it.
A statement of what would change the decision — a fuel hedge, or a regulator delaying the standard — reaches the top of the AO4 band.

common_errors: Arguing that planning is useless in a changing environment, with no distinction between the parts of that environment.
Describing the planning process without judging its usefulness here.

misconceptions.wrong: A profitable business cannot run out of money, so a profitable business does not need a cash-flow forecast.
misconceptions.right: Profit is revenue minus costs over a period; cash flow is money actually entering and leaving the bank in that period. A sale made on 60-day credit is profit today and cash in two months, so a business can be profitable and still be unable to pay a wage bill on Friday. Over-trading is exactly this failure.
misconceptions.probe: A firm sells $80 000 of goods this month on 60-day credit and pays $50 000 of wages and materials this month in cash. State its profit for the month and its net cash flow for the month, and say which of the two determines whether the wages are paid.

misconceptions.wrong: Revenue is what the business earns, so a business with rising revenue is doing better.
misconceptions.right: Revenue is price multiplied by quantity sold, before any cost is taken off. Profit is what is left. Revenue can rise while profit falls, which is what happens when a business discounts to win volume and its contribution per unit falls faster than volume rises.
misconceptions.probe: A shop cuts its price from $20 to $16 and sales rise from 1 000 to 1 300 units. Variable cost is $12 per unit. Calculate revenue before and after, then contribution before and after, and say whether the price cut was worth making.

misconceptions.wrong: Fixed costs never change, so they can be ignored when output changes.
misconceptions.right: Fixed costs do not vary with output over the relevant range, but they do change over time and they step up when the business outgrows its capacity. Fixed cost per unit falls as output rises, which is where economies of scale come from, so fixed costs cannot be ignored when output changes.
misconceptions.probe: Fixed costs are $18 000 a month at outputs up to 30 000 units, and a second production line costing $9 000 a month is needed beyond that. Calculate fixed cost per unit at 25 000 units and at 34 000 units, and explain the jump.

misconceptions.wrong: Break-even output is the output a business should aim to produce.
misconceptions.right: Break-even output is the floor, not the target: at that output profit is exactly zero. The useful figure is the margin of safety, the gap between planned output and break-even, because it says how far demand can fall before the business makes a loss.
misconceptions.probe: Break-even output is 20 000 packs and the business plans to make 30 000. State its profit at break-even, state its margin of safety, and say which of the two numbers you would show to a lender.

misconceptions.wrong: A 50% mark-up on cost is the same as a 50% profit margin.
misconceptions.right: Mark-up is profit as a percentage of cost; margin is profit as a percentage of selling price. A 50% mark-up on a $100 cost gives a $150 price and $50 profit, which is a 33.3% margin. Because the denominators differ, mark-up is always the larger number.
misconceptions.probe: A product costs $100 and is sold at a 50% mark-up. Calculate the selling price, the profit and the profit margin, then say why the margin is not 50%.

misconceptions.wrong: Market share and market growth measure the same thing, so a rising market share means a growing market.
misconceptions.right: Market share is one firm’s sales as a percentage of total market sales; market growth is the change in the size of the whole market. A firm can gain share in a shrinking market and sell fewer units than last year. The Boston matrix uses the two axes precisely because they are independent.
misconceptions.probe: A firm sold $4m in a $40m market last year and $4.4m in a $55m market this year. Calculate its market share in each year and the market growth rate, and say whether the firm is doing better.

misconceptions.wrong: Mentioning the business by name in each paragraph earns the application marks.
misconceptions.right: Application (AO2) is credit for a fact that is true of this business and no other. Cover the business name with your thumb: if the sentence still reads as a textbook statement, it earns nothing. Use a figure, a constraint or a decision from the case instead.
misconceptions.probe: Rewrite this sentence so it would earn an application mark: "Halvara Group could use a differentiation strategy because differentiation allows a business to charge a higher price."

misconceptions.wrong: Adding a judgement at the end of an "Analyse" answer can only help.
misconceptions.right: The command word sets the AO ceiling. "Analyse" is capped at AO3, so there are no evaluation marks on offer; a concluding judgement earns nothing and costs the minutes that a second causal chain would have earned. Judgement belongs in Discuss, Evaluate, Assess and Recommend.
misconceptions.probe: An 8-mark question begins "Analyse the likely effects on...". You have written two chains and have four minutes left. State what you should write next and what you should not, and give the reason in terms of the marks available.

misconceptions.wrong: Paying people more always motivates them.
misconceptions.right: In Herzberg’s two-factor theory pay is a hygiene factor: too little causes dissatisfaction, but adding more does not create satisfaction. Motivators are achievement, recognition, responsibility and the work itself, which is why job enrichment raises motivation where a pay rise only stops complaints.
misconceptions.probe: A call centre raises pay by 8% and labour turnover falls for two months, then returns to its old level. Explain that pattern using Herzberg, and say what the manager should change instead.

misconceptions.wrong: Once a manager delegates a task, responsibility for it has passed to the subordinate.
misconceptions.right: Delegation passes authority to carry out a task; accountability for the outcome stays with the manager. That is why delegation needs clear terms of reference and a review point, and why widening a span of control without training raises risk rather than reducing the manager’s workload.
misconceptions.probe: A regional manager delegates the pricing decision to a branch manager, who prices below cost. Say who is accountable to the board, and name two things the regional manager should have set when delegating.

misconceptions.wrong: A price elasticity of demand of −0.4 is a bigger response than one of −1.4 because −0.4 is closer to zero.
misconceptions.right: PED is normally negative because price and quantity move in opposite directions; what matters is the size, ignoring the sign. Demand is price elastic when the value is beyond −1 and inelastic between 0 and −1. A firm facing elastic demand loses revenue by raising price, and one facing inelastic demand gains it.
misconceptions.probe: Product A has PED −0.4 and product B has PED −1.4. Say which one loses revenue when its price rises by 10%, and calculate the change in quantity demanded for each.

misconceptions.wrong: High gearing is always a sign that a business is in trouble.
misconceptions.right: Gearing measures how much of capital employed is long-term debt. High gearing raises financial risk because interest must be paid whatever profit is, but it also raises returns to shareholders when profit exceeds the interest cost. The judgement depends on interest cover, the stability of cash flow and where interest rates are going.
misconceptions.probe: Two firms both have gearing of 60%. One has interest cover of 8 and steady contract revenue; the other has interest cover of 1.4 and seasonal revenue. Say which is at risk and state the ratio you used to decide.

misconceptions.wrong: The investment with the shortest payback is the most profitable.
misconceptions.right: Payback measures how long the initial outlay takes to be recovered and says nothing about what happens afterwards. A project that pays back in two years and then stops earns less than one that pays back in four and runs for ten. Payback measures liquidity risk; ARR and NPV measure return.
misconceptions.probe: Project X costs $600 000 and returns $300 000 a year for three years. Project Y costs $600 000 and returns $150 000 a year for eight years. Calculate both payback periods, then say which project you would choose and which measure decided it.

misconceptions.wrong: Just-in-time production reduces costs, so any business should adopt it.
misconceptions.right: JIT removes inventory holding costs, but it replaces them with more frequent deliveries, higher ordering costs and no buffer against a supplier failure. It needs reliable suppliers, short lead times and stable demand. Where any of those is missing, a stock-out costs more than the storage that was saved.
misconceptions.probe: A bottling plant 400 km from its only can supplier is considering JIT. State the cost it would save, the two costs it would add, and the single condition that decides whether the change is worth making.

misconceptions.wrong: Every activity in a network has some float, so a short delay never matters.
misconceptions.right: Activities on the critical path have zero float by definition: delaying any of them delays the whole project. Float exists only on non-critical activities, and it is calculated as latest finish time minus earliest start time minus duration.
misconceptions.probe: In a network the critical path runs A–C–E and lasts 13 days. Activity B, which is not on the path, has EST 0, duration 5 and LFT 6. Calculate B’s float, then state the float on A and give the reason.

misconceptions.wrong: Primary research is always better than secondary research because the data is new.
misconceptions.right: Primary data is collected for this decision, so it is current and specific, but it is slow and expensive and a small sample can be unrepresentative. Secondary data is cheap and quick and can size a whole market. Sensible practice is secondary first to frame the question, then primary to answer it.
misconceptions.probe: A skincare firm has three weeks and $4 000 to decide whether to launch in a new country. Say which type of research it should start with and why, and name one risk in the data it will get.

misconceptions.wrong: Stakeholders and shareholders are two words for the owners of the business.
misconceptions.right: Shareholders own part of a company and are one stakeholder group. Stakeholders are everyone affected by the business: employees, customers, suppliers, lenders, government and the local community. Stakeholder conflict exists precisely because these groups want different things from the same decision.
misconceptions.probe: A manufacturer moves production to a cheaper site 60 km away. Name three stakeholder groups affected, state what each gains or loses, and say which group the shareholders are.
